deities: Bhagavathy (Rajarajeswari), worshipped as Saraswathi in the morning, Lakshmi/Bhadrakali at noon, Durga in the evening
Mahavishnu (granite idol beside Bhagavathy; together called Lakshmi Narayana)
Brahma, Siva, Ganapathi, Subramanya and Sastha (idols on the same pedestal)
Dharma Sastha with consorts Purna and Pushkala (north-east shrine)
Bhadrakali at Keezhkkaavu/Kizhukkavu (eastern shrine outside the main temple)
festivals: Makam Thozhal (Makam asterism in the Malayalam month of Kumbham, mid-February to mid-March; the temple's most important festival)

history.dynasty: Chera period origins; later patronage from Cheras, Pandyas, Venadu and Travancore rulers
history.summary: The Chottanikkara Temple, dedicated to Goddess Bhagavathy (Rajarajeswari), is one of the most celebrated Hindu shrines of Kerala, about 17 km from Kochi in Ernakulam district. The original temple is believed to date to the 10th century CE in the Chera period; built largely of wood, it underwent many renovations, with contributions recorded from the Cheras, Pandyas, Venadu and Travancore rulers. The main idol is swayambhu, a self-manifested laterite formation called Rudraksha Sila, said to be untouched by any sculptor; beside it on the same pedestal stands a granite Mahavishnu idol, and the pair are worshipped as Lakshmi Narayana. The goddess is uniquely worshipped in three forms through the day: as Saraswathi draped in white in the morning, as Lakshmi (Bhadrakali) in crimson at noon, and as Durga in blue in the evening. Legend tells of the tribesman Kannappan whose sacrificed calf was spared by his daughter, leading to the discovery of two bleeding divine stones; Vilwamangalam Swamiyar later installed the Bhadrakali idol at Keezhkkaavu, and Adi Shankaracharya is traditionally credited with prescribing the temple's pooja system. The temple is famed for relieving mental afflictions and evil-spirit possession, and its daily Guruthi Pooja at Keezhkkaavu (now performed every evening, earlier only on Fridays) is a distinctive ritual.

name: Chottanikkara Temple
town_description: Kochi (Cochin), on the south-west coast in Ernakulam district, is Kerala's commercial capital and a historic port city known as the 'Queen of the Arabian Sea'. Its landmarks include Fort Kochi with its Chinese fishing nets, Mattancherry Palace and the Paradesi Synagogue, the backwater islands, and a rich blend of Portuguese, Dutch and British colonial heritage. The Chottanikkara Bhagavathy Temple, about 17 km away, is the region's principal Shakti pilgrimage centre.

travel.airport: Cochin International Airport (approx. 36 km; taxis and app cabs available).
travel.railway: Thripunithura Railway Station (approx. 4 km); Ernakulam South Railway Station (approx. 15 km), well connected across India.
travel.road: Approx. 17 km from Kochi/Ernakulam city; easily reached by KSRTC buses, taxis and autos via Thripunithura.

visitor_information.best_time: October to March, when Kerala's weather is cool and pleasant. The Makam Thozhal festival (mid-February to mid-March) is the most spiritually significant time but draws very large crowds.
visitor_information.opening_hours: Morning 4:00 AM to 12:00 noon; evening 4:00 PM to 8:45 PM, open all days (verify - one source lists evening closing at 9:00 PM). No entry fee; footwear not allowed inside. The original swayambhu idol is visible only in the early morning during nirmalyam (around 4 AM).
